nameStory: Spring vetch gets its name from its early blooming habit - it's one of the first members of the vetch family to flower each year. The word 'vetch' comes from the Latin 'vicia,' referring to climbing or sprawling plants in the pea family that were historically used as livestock feed.
description: Spring vetch is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms neat clumps of pointed, compound leaves. In early spring, it produces clusters of purple flowers that gradually fade to a greenish-blue color as they age. This European native is quite rare in New England, forming dense patches about 12-18 inches tall when it does establish itself.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple pea-like flowers bloom in small clusters, starting bright purple then fading to greenish-blue with age - this color change is distinctive among early spring wildflowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 2-3 pairs of pointed oval leaflets that feel smooth to the touch, arranged alternately along the stem without tendrils

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, tidy clumps rather than sprawling like many other vetches - stems are sturdy and upright without the climbing habit of most relatives

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, flat pea pods that turn brown and split open with a slight 'pop' when ripe, releasing smooth round seeds

habitat: Spring vetch prefers rich, well-drained woodland soils and forest edges, often in partially shaded areas. In New England, it's extremely rare and typically found only in cultivated gardens or naturalized around old homesteads where it may have escaped cultivation.

seasonality.spring: Purple flowers appear in April-May before most other wildflowers, making identification easier due to limited competition. New leaves emerge bright green and unfurl quickly.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade to greenish-blue and seed pods develop. Foliage remains lush and green throughout summer heat.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back. Plants begin preparing for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground traces - look for small emerging shoots in very early spring.

funFact: Spring vetch flowers actually change color as they age - starting purple and fading to greenish-blue - which helps the plant signal to bees which flowers still have fresh nectar and which have already been pollinated!
confusionNotes: Most other vetches in New England are climbing plants with tendrils and bloom later in summer, while spring vetch forms upright clumps and blooms very early. The color-changing flowers and early bloom time make it fairly distinctive when present.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'spring vetch,' this plant is more closely related to sweet peas than true vetches, which is why botanists sometimes call it 'spring vetchling' instead. It's primarily known in New England from garden cultivation rather than wild populations.
compareHints: Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea. It also blooms much earlier than summer-flowering relatives like meadow pea and tuberous pea, and forms compact clumps rather than sprawling or climbing.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
